chunks.chunk_text:
Software and consulting are not being replaced by AI in a single clean substitution. They are being unbundled, repriced, and reassembled around systems of execution. The old stack sold seats, billable hours, implementation phases, and expert judgment. The new stack sells outcomes: a workflow that closes, a risk that is continuously monitored, a migration that is mostly automated, a decision that arrives with evidence attached. chunks.chunk_title: The Profit Pool Moves From Labor Arbitrage To Workflow Control
chunks.chunk_text:
Consulting historically monetized uncertainty. Clients paid for decomposition, diagnosis, PMO discipline, implementation labor, and political air cover. Software monetized repeatable capability through licenses or subscriptions. AI collapses part of that distinction. A model-augmented workflow can diagnose, draft, test, reconcile, and execute; the service wrapper becomes thinner unless it owns data access, trust, change management, or governance. This means the restructuring pressure is not against all consultants. It is against undifferentiated leverage: junior research, slide production, boilerplate code, generic benchmarks, template project plans, and run-rate support. The durable value migrates to people and firms that control proprietary context, client authority, regulated trust, integration rights, and measured outcomes. The industry will still buy help. It will buy less performative expertise and more operating systems for judgment. chunks.chunk_title: Developer Productivity Is Real, Uneven, And Easy To Misread
chunks.chunk_text:
The most dangerous boardroom move is to turn AI coding anecdotes into a linear headcount formula. The evidence is mixed by task type, user skill, repository maturity, and evaluation method. A GitHub Copilot controlled experiment found a 55.8% faster completion time on a bounded programming task. METR's 2025 randomized trial found experienced open-source developers were 19% slower when using AI on real issues in large codebases they knew well. Stack Overflow's 2025 survey shows broad interest but also friction: developers complain about answers that are almost right and extra debugging time. The synthesis is simple: AI shifts the bottleneck from typing to specification, context, review, and integration. Companies that redesign the system around AI get leverage. Companies that just add tools to the old process get theater, rework, and inflated productivity stories. chunks.chunk_title: The Software Factory Becomes A Review Factory
chunks.chunk_text:
In the AI software factory, more code is cheap; correct change is still scarce. The center of gravity moves to architecture, product taste, test design, data contracts, security review, and release governance. This is why programmer employment can decline while software-developer employment grows. BLS projects software developers, QA analysts, and testers to grow 15% from 2024 to 2034, but separately projects decline for computer programmers. The distinction matters. AI commoditizes isolated coding tasks faster than it commoditizes accountable engineering. The future engineering organization is smaller in rote implementation, heavier in senior reviewers, domain product managers, platform engineers, SREs, security engineers, and evidence-led QA. The consulting implication is severe: clients will not pay premium rates for large teams that produce artifacts AI can generate. They will pay for judgment that makes generated artifacts safe, coherent, and shippable. chunks.chunk_title: SaaS Moves From Seats To Agents And Outcomes

chunks.chunk_title: The Disruptive Entrant Is The Productized Service
chunks.chunk_text:
The disruptive form is not a chatbot pasted onto a consulting deck. It is a productized service that does one narrow job with a software margin and a service promise: close the books faster, remediate cloud waste, reconcile vendor contracts, generate migration tests, classify regulatory obligations, or draft an RFP with evidence. At first, incumbents dismiss these as subscale tools. Then the tools collect workflow data, harden templates, standardize integrations, and move upmarket. Christensen's pattern repeats: the entrant begins where gross margins are unattractive to the incumbent, improves through use, and eventually attacks the main profit pool. The consulting firm that treats AI as an internal efficiency program misses the strategic threat. The threat is a new product category that turns repeatable advisory work into an executable system. chunks.chunk_title: A Grove Inflection: The Basis Of Competition Changes
chunks.chunk_text:
Grove's question is not whether AI is useful. It is whether the basis of competition has changed. In software and consulting, the old basis was reputation, installed base, partner ecosystem, implementation capacity, and control of scarce expertise. The new basis adds model access, proprietary data, evaluation harnesses, governance controls, agent orchestration, and the ability to learn from every completed workflow. The incumbent danger is denial by good results. Spending is up, bookings exist, and clients still need help. That can mask the inflection. chunks.chunk_title: The Thompson Lens: Distribution Eats Advisory

Consultants once had privileged distribution: senior relationships, procurement access, industry frameworks, and armies that could turn a board decision into workstreams. chunks.chunk_title: Labor Does Not Vanish; It Recombines
chunks.chunk_text:
The labor story is not mass disappearance on one date. It is recombination. BLS projects strong growth for management analysts and software roles even as coding-only programming declines. WEF and ILO both frame AI as a mixture of automation, augmentation, displacement, and new-skill demand. This fits the observed enterprise pattern: companies want more AI engineers, data engineers, workflow owners, compliance leads, and product-minded operators. They need fewer people doing low-context preparation work. The junior apprenticeship model is therefore the fault line. Consulting and software firms historically trained seniors by overstaffing juniors on repeatable work. chunks.chunk_title: The Counterpositioned Buyer Will Insist On Outcome Pricing
chunks.chunk_text:
AI gives buyers a new argument: if delivery is AI-accelerated, why should pricing remain hour-based or seat-based? Procurement teams will push for outcome pricing, consumption bands, success fees, and lower run-rate support costs. Services firms will resist because utilization, leverage, and rate cards are deeply embedded in their operating systems. SaaS vendors will resist because seat expansion has been the cleanest path to net revenue retention. The negotiation will be uneven. Vendors with scarce data, workflow lock-in, regulatory trust, or platform gravity can defend price. Vendors selling generic capacity will be re-benchmarked. This is where AbarVa's worldview matters: the buyer does not need to believe all consulting disappears. The buyer only needs enough machine leverage and benchmark transparency to reset the anchor price. The strong opposing case has five parts. First, demand may outrun automation: Gartner, BLS, and company reports show expanding IT services, software, software roles, and management analyst work. The first restructuring wave hits work with high text density, repeatable patterns, weak tacit context, and low regulatory finality: proposal drafts, discovery synthesis, status reporting, test generation, code translation, documentation, requirements summarization, ticket triage, knowledge-base operations, benchmark research, and first-pass financial or operational analysis. The second wave hits repeatable managed services where agents can monitor, classify, remediate, and escalate.
